extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, administrative law scholars, social researchers, and officials concerned with unemployment insurance investigation and overpayment procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and description of Unemployment Insurance Commission (UIC) benefit-control interview practices, investigation/reporting standards, and policies for identifying, notifying, and recovering overpayments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview location rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are to be on UIC premises . . . unless there is evidence to suggest that a field investigation or residence interview is necessary to establish the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field/residence interviews appropriate when on-premises interviews are doubtful of success (e.g., claimant did not report, suspected self-employment, suspected found work) or for rural/sparsely populated remote areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party presence during interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may only intervene in the interview in order to advise or assist the claimant or to act as an interpreter, if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for interpreters, third parties are not allowed to act as the claimant's representative. If a third party's presence makes a reasonable interview impossible, BCOs must agree on another interview date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and disclosure in field/third-party interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: BCOs are required to identify themselves and the purpose of their visit to the claimant in field interviews; in third-party interviews it is left to the BCO's discretion whether disclosure of the purpose is likely to cause embarrassment to the claimant or third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCO must judge whether informing third parties of the inquiry's purpose would cause embarrassment and may refrain accordingly; this discretion is explicitly permitted by the guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to warn about criminal implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC contends that its officers are not required to warn claimants of the consequences of their statements in terms of criminal prosecution because refusal to answer does not make a claimant liable to criminal sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated UIC policy/position on warnings in suspected-fraud investigations; it frames whether BCOs must give advance warning of possible criminal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of failure to attend interview and locating absent claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimant fails to attend an interview, he is disentitled by the Agent II under sec. 54(1) and 55(6) of the Act; if the BCO cannot locate the claimant in serious suspected offences, he will request help from the Data Centre which retains claim-file data for three years and contact recovery sections for possible 'recidivists'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs should use Data Centre resources and regional recovery units to locate claimants, especially when offences warrant more extensive investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity verification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The BCO first verifies the identity of the interviewee by asking for his Social Insurance Card and comparing the number and the signature thereon with those on the application for benefit; he then also asks the claimant to verify the authenticity of the application form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard initial step to authenticate claimant identity and application authenticity before substantive questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing technique: encourage claimant talk; minimize interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The BCO questions the claimant, endeavouring to get him to talk and to let him talk by limiting his own interventions to a bare minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective is to gather sufficiently conclusive information for Agent II decisions. BCOs may use subtle or psychological techniques (e.g., trick questions), but excessive leading or distortive questioning is criticized (see anti-patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics to cover in a general control interview
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting a general control of the claimant's situation, the BCO covers in succession: (a) capability of working; (b) availability; (c) employment sought; (d) financial situation; (e) job search; (f) self-employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each topic includes detailed subquestions: (a) reasons for leaving employment, health, work since application, rehire chances, job skills; (b) travel outside region, child-care arrangements, courses/training, pregnancy confinement date, union status, last visit to country of origin, personal business; (c) type of work sought, suitable hours, minimum salary, location requirements; (d) family/financial responsibilities, other income sources; (e) employers contacted, dates/types of contact, reasons for refusal, scope of search; (f) agricultural/professional/business activities devoted to since applying. The topics should be covered to assemble a full factual picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading questions and twisting replies
rubrics_metrics.description: BCOs have been criticized for making use of leading questions and subsequently twisting the meaning of replies by making them much more categorical than they had actually been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverse example: asking 'I suppose a minimum wage of $3.25 an hour would suit you?' and later reporting claimant demanded $3.25. Investigation/reporting should distinguish between claimant hopes/speculation and categorical assertions; BCOs should not reframe or exaggerate claimant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling contradictory statements
rubrics_metrics.description: If statements are contradictory, the BCO may telephone third parties to request additional information; if contradiction persists, he must endeavour to settle the matter by questioning the claimant, the third party, or both; if still unresolved, he must give both versions in his investigation report, together with an account of his attempts to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCO must document steps taken to clarify contradictions; unresolved contradictions should be recorded transparently in the report with an account of investigative efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of observations in residence interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting interview outside the UIC office, particularly at the claimant's residence, the BCO may obtain information by observing the claimant's family, his way of life and his visible activities in addition to questioning him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such observations (physical state, family attitude, activities at home) are particularly useful for determining eligibility for sickness benefit. Observational evidence complements questioning but must be integrated responsibly into the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for 'statement from the claimant' (pre-1975 practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement from a claimant is a record of his admissions or denials of matters on which he was questioned; it was intended to be written in the first person, reflect voluntary consent, contain an accurate but concise account of the claimant's position, precise information (dates, times, amounts), and be written in simple language without technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: BCO completes statement in duplicate, reads it to claimant, obtains agreement and signature (and interpreter's), makes justified corrections at claimant's request, and gives claimant one copy whether signed or not. If claimant refuses to sign/accept, BCO must indicate this on the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and style requirements for the Report of Investigation (pre-1975)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Report of Investigation allowed the BCO to summarize results, bring out key information from other sources and the claimant's statement, supplement with assessment and recommend sanctions; UIC Manual (sec. 501.6.2) stipulated reports should be written impartially, report facts including those in claimant's favour, clearly distinguish opinions/surmises from facts, and contain all details necessary to be fully understood by someone with no knowledge of the claimant's situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports could be handwritten except where criminal prosecution recommended (then typed); prepared in duplicate; included space to note actions taken as result of recommendations (entitlement, overpayment amounts, administrative penalties). BCOs in practice often wrote telegraphic summaries and sometimes expressed opinions without full justification; production pressures (20–40 investigations/week unofficial quota) may affect quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for the Report of Interview (post-1975)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Report of Interview must present factual information gathered during the investigation and especially during the interview; it should contain no assessment or expression of opinion by the BCO and is signed only by the BCO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCO must indicate 'pertinent information' and either have the claimant read the report or read it to him and make corrections the claimant requests; if BCO disagrees with claimant's changes, he must record his comments separately. The report is prepared in duplicate and claimant receives one copy (refusal to accept must be noted). The form contains a printed sentence stating the report was explained to the claimant and will be reviewed by an Insurance Agent; the UIC's position is that the information is satisfactory as evidence without claimant's endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/confidentiality of sanction recommendations and decision authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The BCO's recommendations with regard to sanctions are transmitted separately and the claimant is not made aware of them; the decision-making authority about entitlement, administrative penalties, or criminal prosecution lies with the Agent II (and for prosecutions concurrence of District Manager and Regional Legal Counsel is required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Files involving recommended criminal prosecution are forwarded through supervisory and legal channels for concurrence before substantive Agent II decision; BCOs may recommend penalties but Agent II may accept, modify, or refuse to impose them.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCO authority to suspend payments and request recoupment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the abuse revealed by the investigation extends over some time, the BCO is authorized to forward to the Regional Pay Centre an order to suspend payment of benefit; if it is an isolated incident, the BCO is authorized to request the Overpayment Section to recoup the amount of overpayment from benefits payable in accordance with sec. 49(3) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs have limited operational authority to initiate interim administrative actions to protect program funds, with recoupment actions channeled through appropriate units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overpayment determination steps and causes classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination that benefits have been paid in excess involves: discovery/establishment of existence and amount; informing the claimant; deciding how to deal with the overpayment. Overpayments are categorized under headings: (A) earnings and employment; (B) availability and capability; (C) recomputation due to additional information; (D) duplicate payments; (E) renewal on non-renewable claim; (F) inactive search for work; (G) other. They are also classified as 'fraud' or 'non-fraud' depending on penalties or court costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include claimant misrepresentation, claimant misunderstanding/inadequate information, UIC official error, or delay/automation syncing issues. Overpayment amounts and typical discovery mechanisms (audits, BCOs, data reviews, coding errors) are described. Labels such as sex/marital status may be added for collection-method informational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification content and claimant information about overpayments
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an overpayment is discovered, a letter informs the claimant about the overpayment and indicates how the amount the UIC considers is owing can be repaid to the Commission's satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, claimants are often unaware of overpayments and of the range of recovery methods and UIC discretion (reduced repayments, write-offs). Pamphlets ('Rights and Obligations', 'Appeal Procedure') warn claimants to avoid overpayments and note that Insurance Officers may decide an overpayment occurred, but overpayment determinations themselves are not appealable. The report notes a lack of disclosure to claimants about UIC errors and limited ability to challenge collection methods before an objective body.
